questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence. If there is no need to substitute it, select ‘No substitution required’.**

__Nalini was not satisfy with her birthday dress__, but she wore it anyway.

options.text: Nalini was not satisfied for her birthday dress
Nalini was not satisfied with her birthday dress
Nalini were not satisfied by her birthday dress

questions.solution:
The correct answer is **'Nalini was not satisfied with her birthday dress'.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The underlined part in the given sentence is grammatically incorrect.
 
• Here, **'Nalini was not satisfied with her birthday dress'** should be used instead of** 'Nalini was not satisfy with her birthday dress'.**
 
• **"Nalini was not satisfy" **is incorrect because** "satisfy"** is **a verb** in** the present tense**, but in this context, it needs to be in the **past tense** to match with **"was."** The correct past participle form of the verb **"satisfy"** is **"satisfied."**
 
• Here's a breakdown of the correction:
 
 
• *"**Nalini**" is the subject.*
 
• *"**was**" is the past tense form of the verb "**to be.**"*
 
• *"**not satisfied**" is the past participle form of the verb "**satisfy**" used to match **the past tense of "was."***
 
 
 
• When using the verb** "to be"** (in this case,** "was"**) in *the past tense*, we need to pair it with **a past participle form** of **the verb** that follows it. Therefore, the correct form should be *"Nalini was not satisfied."*

 

**Correct Sentence:__** ***Nalini was not satisfied with her birthday dress**, but she wore it anyway.*

questions.question:
**Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.**

White elephant

options.text: Something that costs a lot of money but has no useful purpose
A big lie that is concealed from all

questions.solution:
The correct answer is option 2, **"Something that costs a lot of money but has no useful purpose."**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The idiom **"white elephant"** refers to something that is expensive but useless or burdensome.
 
• It comes from a tradition in some cultures of giving rare and valuable white elephants as gifts, which were difficult and costly to care for.
 
 
• *Example: "My grandfather's antique car collection is a white elephant because it costs so much to maintain and we never use them."*
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• Origin of this idiom: 
 
 
• The origin of the idiom **"white elephant" **dates back to ancient Southeast Asia, particularly to regions like Thailand, Myanmar, Laos, and Cambodia. In these areas, white elephants were considered sacred and held great significance.
 
• **White elephants **were **extremely rare**, and their appearance was seen as a symbol of prestige and divine favor. They were often owned by monarchs and were considered sacred, embodying power, wealth, and prosperity. However, due to their sacred status, they couldn't be used for regular work or practical purposes.
 
• Owning a **white elephant **became an expensive affair as it required specific care, attention, and resources without offering any practical benefits. It was an honor to possess one, but maintaining it could become a financial burden. Moreover, giving away or disposing of a gift as esteemed as a white elephant was considered disrespectful.
 
• This idea evolved into the modern idiom** "white elephant," **which refers to something rare or prestigious that is costly to maintain or has little practical use. It denotes an object or property that is expensive and challenging to maintain but offers little or no value or benefit in return.
 
• Over time, the term **"white elephant"** transitioned from its literal meaning as a sacred and rare animal to a metaphorical expression used to describe expensive or burdensome possessions or projects.

• "**Whale**" is a large marine mammal and doesn't relate to the time it took to fix the hole in the wall.
 
• "**Hold**" means to grasp or keep something in position, but it doesn't fit in the sentence contextually.
 
• "**Whole**" refers to the entirety or complete amount of something. In the sentence, *"It took a whole day for them to do the job" *indicates that it took an entire day from start to finish to complete the task of fixing the hole in the wall.
